_note: Speaking A1–B2, one entry per task, same shape as its two neighbours in this folder.
The picture descriptions are grouped into `sets` of four (picture series), the way the
vocabulary sets are: one sitting, one subject area, not a level's whole inventory.
Sixteen pictures listed flat is a scroll; four under a heading you chose is an exercise
you finish. Tasks that are not pictures (introducing yourself, the talk, the discussion,
planning together) stay outside the sets: they are one-offs, not a series.
No exam name in a title. A picture description is a thing you practise whether or not
you ever sit an exam. Where the exam relevance is real it lives in `exam`, one quiet line
at the foot of the task page (src/pages/sprechen/[id].astro keys it by its text).
Every model answer describes the photo that is on disk (public/assets/sprechen/), not
an imagined one. `imageNeeded` describes that photo too: it is what the page shows if the
file is missing. Do not point these at a stock URL: the site's images are its own.
Entries marked `from` borrow an existing picture and its questions: `sprechen-dtz` the
three pictures of src/data/sprechen.json (follow-up questions as a second timed half),

sets.title: At home and in the neighbourhood
sets.blurb: Four pictures from everyday life close to home: kitchen, shop, station, park.

sets.title: Out and about, together
sets.blurb: Four pictures in which several people are doing something together.

sets.title: Work and public offices
sets.blurb: Four situations to do with work, job interviews and offices.

sets.title: City, environment, world of work
sets.blurb: Four pictures you have to give an opinion on, not just describe.

tasks.title: Introducing yourself
tasks.blurb: The very first speaking task, and the one you need most often in everyday life.
tasks.imageNeeded: A classroom: a teacher is writing on a whiteboard, a student sits in front of it. Friendly, everyday.
tasks.prompt: Introduce yourself. Talk about yourself for one minute.
bullets: Name
Age
Country / home town
Where you live now
Languages
Job
Family
Free time
phrases: My name is … / I'm …
I'm … years old.
I'm from … and now I live in …
I speak … and a little English.
I'm a … / I work as a …
I've got … children. / I'm single.
In my free time I …
tasks.model: Hello, my name is Amir Sadat. I'm 29 years old and I'm from Herat. That's in Afghanistan. Now I live in Leeds. I speak Dari, Pashto and a little English. I'm an electrician. I'm married and I've got a daughter. In my free time I play football.
check: All eight points come up.
Full sentences, not a list: “I'm 29 years old.”, not just “29”. A job needs a or an: “I'm an electrician.”
End with your free time: the examiner often asks the next question about it.
tasks.exam: The usual first part of a speaking test: introducing yourself.

tasks.title: At the station
tasks.blurb: Who? Where? What is the person doing? Three questions, three sentences.
tasks.imageNeeded: A railway platform: a woman with a suitcase and a big bag walks past a white and blue train. A station sign on the wall. Few people.
tasks.prompt: What can you see in the picture? Say three to five sentences.
bullets: Who is in the picture?
Where is she?
What is she doing? What has she got with her?
What colour is the train?
Do you often travel by train? Where do you go?
phrases: I can see a woman / a man.
She's at the station.
She's got a suitcase.
She's walking to the train.
I think she's going on holiday.
tasks.model: In the picture I can see a woman at a train station. She's got a suitcase and a big bag, and she's holding a cup of coffee. She's walking to the train. The train is white and blue. I think she's going on holiday. I sometimes travel by train too, for example to Manchester.
check: “I can see …” is the easiest way to start, and it is always right.
“I think …” and “maybe …” let you guess without being sure.
The last sentence is about you: that is what the examiner asks next.

tasks.title: In the kitchen
tasks.blurb: A man, a child, a meal: words you use every day at home.
tasks.imageNeeded: A small kitchen: a man is cooking at the cooker, a little girl sits on the worktop next to him and watches. Flowers by the sink.
tasks.prompt: What can you see in the picture? Say three to five sentences.
bullets: How many people are in the picture?
Where are they?
What are they doing?
What is the man cooking, do you think?
Who cooks in your home? What do you like cooking?
phrases: There are two people in the picture.
They're in the kitchen.
The man is cooking.
The girl is sitting next to him.
At home I usually cook …
tasks.model: There are two people in the picture: a man and a little girl. They're in the kitchen. The man is cooking and the girl is sitting next to him. She's watching him. Maybe he's her dad. At home I usually cook. I like cooking rice with vegetables.
check: First count (“two people”), then say the place, then the action. This order always works.
For what is happening now, use is + -ing: is cooking, is sitting, is watching.
The end is about you.

tasks.title: At the supermarket
tasks.blurb: Shopping: food words, numbers and how to pay.
tasks.imageNeeded: A supermarket checkout: a young woman and a young man are packing their shopping into a paper bag; the cashier is on the left. A pineapple on the counter.
tasks.prompt: What can you see in the picture? Say three to five sentences.
bullets: Where are the people?
What are they buying?
What is the cashier doing?
In your country, do people pay in cash or by card?
Where do you go shopping? How often?
phrases: They're at the checkout.
They're buying fruit and vegetables.
The cashier is on the left.
I pay by card / in cash.
I go shopping once a week.
tasks.model: I can see a supermarket. A young woman and a young man are at the checkout. They're buying some fruit. I can see a pineapple. The man is putting the shopping in a paper bag. The cashier is on the left. I go to the supermarket once a week, usually on Saturday. I always pay by card.
check: Food words in the plural: apples, bananas, vegetables. But some fruit, some bread: no plural.
“at the checkout”, “by card”, “in cash”: learn the little word with the phrase.
A time phrase at the end (“on Saturday”, “once a week”) sounds practised straight away.

tasks.title: In the park
tasks.blurb: A child, an adult, the weather, and your first chance to use “because”.
tasks.imageNeeded: A playground in a park: a boy and a woman sit together on a big round swing and smile. Lots of trees, a sunny day.
tasks.prompt: What can you see in the picture? Say three to five sentences.
bullets: Who is in the picture?
Where are they?
What are they doing?
What's the weather like?
Do you like going to the park? What do you do there?
phrases: I can see a boy and a woman.
They're in the park.
They're sitting on a swing.
The weather is nice.
I like going to the park because …
tasks.model: In the picture I can see a boy and a woman. They're in a park, at a playground. They're sitting on a big swing and they're smiling. Maybe she's his mum. There are lots of trees and the weather is nice. I like going to the park because it's quiet there.
check: Two people, two sentences: first the boy, then the woman.
One sentence about the weather: the examiner almost always asks.
“because” joins your reason to your sentence: I like the park because it's quiet.

tasks.title: Working together outdoors
tasks.blurb: Describe, guess, and then talk about your own life.
tasks.exam: A task type from picture-based speaking tests.
phrases: In the picture you can see …
I think they work at …
She's wearing …
I haven't got a garden, but …
In my country …
check: First describe, then guess: who the two people could be and where they are.
Answer the follow-up questions in full sentences, not just yes or no.
One reason with “because”: at A2 one is enough, but it must be there.
tasks.model: In the picture I can see two people between lots of small green trees. Maybe it's a garden centre. The woman is wearing gloves and she's holding a spray bottle. The man is wearing blue work clothes and he's holding garden scissors. They're both laughing, so I think they enjoy their work. I think they work there, because the man has got a name badge. I haven't got a garden, but I grow tomatoes and herbs on my balcony.

tasks.title: People on a bus
tasks.blurb: Describe a mood, and say how you get to work yourself.
tasks.exam: A task type from picture-based speaking tests.
phrases: At the front there's …, behind him …
The people look tired.
Maybe they're going home.
I usually go to work by …
On the bus I like listening to …
check: Don't just say who is sitting where: say what the mood is and how you can tell.
In the follow-up questions, talk about your own day: how long, how often, how.
Use time phrases: in the morning, every day, about twenty minutes.
tasks.model: In the picture you can see a bus with lots of passengers. At the front there's an older man in a blue hat. Behind him there are young and older people. Nobody is talking. Most of them are just looking in front of them. They look tired. Maybe they're going home after work. I go to work by bus every day too. It takes about twenty minutes. On the bus I usually listen to music or read the news.

tasks.title: A meal in the garden
tasks.blurb: Lots of people in one picture, and the question of why they are there.
tasks.imageNeeded: A long table in a garden with food and drinks. People of different ages are eating together and talking; an older woman in a red cardigan is laughing.
tasks.imageQuery: neighbours eating together outdoor garden party
tasks.prompt: Describe the picture. Then say what you think about the situation.
bullets: How many people can you see? Who could they be?
Where is this, and what time of day is it?
What are the people doing?
Why do people meet for a meal like this?
Do you know your neighbours? What are they like?
Do people do this in your country too?
phrases: In the foreground there's …, in the background …
The people seem to know each other well.
I think it's a family party, because …
In my street / my building …
In my country it's different: …
tasks.model: In the picture I can see a long table in a garden. There's a lot of food on it, and some glasses and drinks. About six people are sitting at the table. In the middle there's an older woman in a red cardigan. She's laughing. Next to her there are some young people. I think it's a family party, because there are old and young people together. Maybe it's the grandmother's birthday. I think a meal like this is great, because everyone has time to talk. In my country we often eat together outside in summer, but usually with the family, not with the neighbours.
check: Say what is in the foreground and in the background: that is the step from A1 to A2.
A guess with a reason: “I think it's …, because …”
End with a comparison with your own life or country. At A2 the examiner almost always asks.

tasks.title: At the doctor's
tasks.blurb: Waiting, appointments, being nervous, and how to talk about how someone feels.
tasks.imageNeeded: A doctor's waiting room: a woman in a dark suit sits on a chair and looks up at a doctor in a white coat, who is holding a folder.
tasks.prompt: Describe the picture. Then say what you think about the situation.
bullets: Where are the people?
What do they look like? What are they doing?
How does the woman feel, do you think?
How long do you usually wait for a doctor's appointment?
What do you do when you are ill? Do you go to a doctor or a pharmacy first?
phrases: The woman is sitting in the waiting room.
On the left there's a doctor. He's / She's holding …
She looks a bit worried.
Maybe the doctor has got her test results.
I usually wait about … for an appointment.
tasks.model: The picture shows a waiting room at a doctor's. A young woman is sitting on a grey chair. She's wearing a dark suit. On the left there's a doctor in a white coat. We can only see the doctor's arm and a yellow folder. The woman is looking up at the doctor. She looks a bit worried. Maybe the doctor has got her test results. When I'm ill, I usually phone my doctor first. I often wait two or three weeks for an appointment. I think that's quite long.
check: Say how someone feels and why: “She looks worried. Maybe …” Pictures with people almost always get this question.
Say what you can and can't see: “We can only see the doctor's arm.”
A real detail from your own life (“two or three weeks”) is worth more than a general sentence.

tasks.title: Two people in the park
tasks.blurb: Interpret a situation; don't just list what you can see.
tasks.exam: A task type from picture-based speaking tests.
phrases: It looks as if …
I'd guess that they …, because …
It's probably …
I think it's important that …
When I was younger, I used to …
check: Interpret, don't just describe: who are the two people, and what have they just done?
An opinion with a reason: at B1, “I think it's … because …” works well.
For “Have you ever …?” tell a short story in the past, with one example.
tasks.model: In the picture a young man and an older woman are walking through a park together. They're both wearing sports clothes and they've got towels round their necks. He's holding a water bottle. It looks as if they've just done some exercise together. He's got his arm round her shoulders and she's laughing. I'd guess they're mother and son, because they seem so close. It's probably summer, because the trees are green. I think it's really nice when young and older people do things together, because both of them get something out of it. When I was younger, I used to help my grandmother with her shopping every week.

tasks.title: The job interview
tasks.blurb: Two sides of a table, and the question of who is the nervous one.
tasks.imageNeeded: A bright office with a big window: a young woman and a man in a suit sit opposite each other at a table, with a laptop and papers. A plant between them.
tasks.prompt: Describe the picture and then talk about the topic.
bullets: Who is sitting where, and who could be who?
What is the atmosphere like?
How do you prepare for a job interview?
Which questions are almost always asked?
Have you ever had a job interview in English?
What is different about applying for a job in your country?
phrases: On the left there's …, opposite her …
You can tell from … that he's the interviewer.
I'd guess that …
In my opinion, the most important thing is …
When I applied for my first job, …
tasks.model: The picture shows an office with a big window. On the left there's a young woman, and opposite her there's a man in a dark suit with glasses. There's a laptop and some papers on the table. I'd guess it's a job interview. The man is probably the interviewer, because the laptop and the papers are in front of him. The woman is smiling, but she might be a bit nervous. To prepare for an interview, you should find out about the company, think about answers to the usual questions and get your documents ready. They almost always ask about your strengths and why you want this job. When I applied for my first job in English, I was very nervous because I was afraid of making mistakes. Now I know that most employers care more about whether you can do the job.
check: Use place words to organise what you say: on the left, on the right, opposite, in the background.
Show that a guess is a guess (“I'd guess that …”, “might be”) and give a reason.
The part in the past (“When I applied …, I was …”) is expected at B1, not optional.
One sentence with “In my opinion”: giving your opinion is the real B1 part.

tasks.title: In the workshop
tasks.blurb: Apprenticeships, skilled trades, and why fewer young people choose them.
tasks.imageNeeded: A workshop: an older worker with grey hair works at a metal bench, a young man stands next to him and watches. Work clothes, a real workshop.
tasks.prompt: Describe the picture and then talk about the topic.
bullets: What kind of place is this?
What are the two people doing?
What is an apprenticeship?
Why do fewer young people want to learn a trade today?
What job did you learn? How did you learn it?
phrases: It seems to be a workshop.
The older man is showing the young man how to …
An apprentice works for a company and also studies.
One reason could be that …
I trained as a …
tasks.model: The picture seems to show a workshop. There are two people at a metal bench: an older man with grey hair and a young man in a black T-shirt. The older man is working with his hands, and the young man is watching carefully. I suppose the older man is teaching him, because the young man is standing very close and following every move. Maybe he's an apprentice. An apprentice works for a company and earns money, and at the same time they study, for example at a college. But today fewer young people choose this way. One reason could be that many of them prefer to go to university, because they hope to earn more later. I trained as an electrician myself, and I think in a trade you can see very quickly what you have done.
check: “I suppose …, because …” joins a guess and a reason in one sentence.
Explain a word (apprenticeship, trade) instead of just saying it.
The “why” question gets a real answer with “because” or “One reason could be that …”.

tasks.title: At the front desk
tasks.blurb: Forms, appointments, waiting, and how to talk about it without just complaining.
tasks.imageNeeded: A front desk in an office: a member of staff with a tablet talks to a visitor across the counter. Light, plain room.
tasks.prompt: Describe the picture and then talk about the topic.
bullets: Where are the people, and how can you tell?
What are they doing?
For what kind of things do people go to an office like this, for example at the council?
What is difficult about official forms and offices when English isn't your first language?
Think of a time you had to sort something out at an office. What happened?
phrases: You can tell from … that she works there.
The visitor seems to be asking about …
You usually need an appointment for …
The most difficult thing is that …
When I first came here, …
tasks.model: In the picture two women are talking at a front desk. You can tell that the woman on the left works there, because she's standing behind the counter and holding a tablet. The other woman is a visitor. She's smiling, so I think the conversation is going well. Maybe she's asking about an appointment or a form. People go to offices like this for lots of things, for example at the council for a parking permit or a question about council tax. The most difficult thing is often the language on the forms, because there are lots of words you never hear in everyday life. When I first came here, I filled in a form wrongly and had to do it again three times. Now I just ask at the desk when I don't understand something.
check: Show how you know something: “You can tell that …, because …”
Give a real example from your own life instead of a general complaint.
“Now I …” shows how things have changed: examiners like to hear that at B1.

tasks.title: Talk: Helping without being paid
tasks.blurb: Photo, talk, discussion: the three stages on one topic.
tasks.exam: A task type from speaking tests at B1 and B2.

tasks.title: Discussion: Volunteering at school
tasks.blurb: Take a position, deal with the counter-argument, and stand your ground.
tasks.exam: A task type from speaking tests at B2.

tasks.title: Planning together: a leaving party at work
tasks.blurb: Suggest, disagree, agree: the task where you react rather than present.
tasks.prompt: A colleague is retiring after eleven years. With another person, plan the leaving party. Talk about all the points, make suggestions, react to the other person's suggestions and agree on a plan at the end.
bullets: When and where should the party be?
Who should you invite: just your team or the whole company?
Food and drink: make it yourselves or order it?
A present: what, and who collects the money?
Who will make the speech?
phrases: I'd suggest that we …
How about …? / What if we …?
I see what you mean, but …
I'm not sure about that, because …
Can we agree that …?
Right, so we've agreed: …
tasks.model:
— I'd suggest that we have the party on the last Friday of the month, straight after work. Then nobody has to come in specially.
— I see what you mean, but on Fridays half the team have already left for the weekend. How about Thursday?
— Fine, Thursday's better. And where? The canteen, or would you rather go to a restaurant?
— I'd go for the canteen. It doesn't cost anything and we can decorate it ourselves. But I'd order the food, otherwise one person ends up alone in the kitchen again.
— Right, so we've agreed: Thursday, the canteen, and we'll order the food. That leaves the present.
— She loves plants. What if I collect the money from the team and you buy the present?
— Deal. And I think Mr Demir should make the speech. He's worked with her the longest.
check: You react to the other person instead of working through your own list.
Disagree politely at least once: that is what the task tests.
At the end you clearly agree on every point.
Polite forms with would and could: I'd suggest, I'd go for, could we …?
tasks.exam: A task type from paired speaking tests at B1 and B2.

tasks.title: Market or supermarket?
tasks.blurb: A friendly picture, and the question of who can afford it.
tasks.imageNeeded: A market stall full of lettuce and green vegetables under a green awning; an older customer in a pink shirt, a stallholder reaching across. Morning light.
tasks.prompt: Describe the picture briefly and then give your opinion.
bullets: What can you see in the picture?
What impression does the scene give?
What are the advantages of shopping at a market rather than a supermarket?
What are the arguments against it?
Is buying local food a question of principle or of money?
How do you do your own shopping, and why?
phrases: In the foreground there's …, and behind it …
The scene gives the impression that …
One clear advantage of … is that …
On the other hand, …
We shouldn't forget that …
In the end, it depends on whether …
tasks.model: In the foreground there's a market stall piled high with lettuce and other green vegetables, and behind it an older man in a pink shirt is looking at what's on offer. The stallholder is reaching across to him, so they seem to be in the middle of a conversation. The scene gives the impression that shopping here is slower and more personal: you don't just buy things, you talk to the people who sell them. One clear advantage of a market is that the food hasn't travelled as far, and you can find out where it comes from. On the other hand, markets are often only open when most people are at work: if you finish at six, the stalls have already gone. We also shouldn't forget that prices are usually higher. So buying local isn't only a question of principle, it's also a question of income and working hours. I do most of my shopping at the supermarket and go to the market on Saturdays if I can. To be honest, that's out of convenience, not principle.
check: The description is short. At B2 it is the way in, not the task.
Both sides are there, with the linking words for them: one clear advantage, on the other hand, we shouldn't forget.
Saying “not only …, it's also …” shows you have really thought the question through.
The personal ending is honest rather than perfect: that is harder to say and sounds more mature.

tasks.title: Half in the room, half on screen
tasks.blurb: Some people in the room, one on the screen, and who gets left out.
tasks.imageNeeded: A meeting room or small hall: a woman with a microphone speaks at the front; behind her a big screen shows a person joining by video. People in the foreground are watching.
tasks.imageQuery: hybrid meeting room video conference screen
tasks.prompt: Describe the picture briefly and then give your opinion.
bullets: What kind of situation does the picture show?
Who is in the room, and who is joining online?
What are the advantages of hybrid working?
What are the disadvantages for the people who join online?
Should companies tell staff which days to be in the office?
How would you most like to work?
phrases: The picture obviously shows …
What strikes me is that …
A clear advantage is that …
The problem, in my view, is that …
Some people might argue that …
Personally, I'd …
tasks.model: The picture obviously shows a meeting or a talk where some people are in the room and at least one person is joining by video. At the front a woman is speaking into a microphone, and behind her the person on the big screen is listening. In the foreground we can see the backs of two people in the audience. What strikes me is that everyone is looking at the woman with the microphone, not at the screen. A clear advantage of hybrid working is that people save time travelling and can fit work around their family more easily. The problem, in my view, is that the people who join online are at a disadvantage: they miss the chat before and after the meeting, and if they want to say something, they have to wait for a gap. Some people might argue that a good chair can solve this, but in practice that rarely happens by itself. So I think fixed office days for the whole team make more sense than a rule for every single person. Personally, I'd like to work two days in the office and three at home.
check: Something you notice in the picture supports your argument (“What strikes me is that …”), not just general knowledge.
The objection to your own view is there (“Some people might argue …”) and you answer it.
The difference between “fixed office days for the team” and “a rule for every person” is a fine distinction. That is exactly what separates B2 from B1.

tasks.title: Building work in town
tasks.blurb: Diggers, noise, new flats, and the question of who a town is for.
tasks.imageNeeded: A building site in a town: a yellow digger in front of new blocks of flats, a white van, piles of sand. Daylight.
tasks.prompt: Describe the picture briefly and then give your opinion.
bullets: What can you see in the picture?
What does a building site like this mean for the people who live nearby and for local shops?
Why do towns build so many new flats?
How should a town involve the people who are affected?
Is there a similar project where you live? What do people say about it?
phrases: In the centre of the picture there's …
What you notice first is …
For people who live nearby, this means …
On the other hand, you could argue that …
The real question is not whether …, but how …
In my town, they're currently …
tasks.model: In the centre of the picture there's a big yellow digger on a building site, and behind it there are some new blocks of flats with balconies. On the left there's a white van, and the ground is covered in sand and stones. What you notice first is how close the site is to the flats: people are clearly already living there. For people who live nearby, a site like this means months of noise, dust and lorries. For local shops it can mean fewer customers, because the street is harder to get to. On the other hand, you could argue that towns have no choice: there aren't enough homes, and you can't build new ones without building sites. In my view, the real question is not whether a town should build, but how: whether the people nearby are told early, whether the work is done at reasonable times, and whether the timetable is kept. In my town, they're currently building flats on an old car park, and that's exactly what people argue about. Nobody is against new homes; they're against the noise starting at seven in the morning.
check: A detail from the picture (the flats right next to the site) becomes part of the argument, not just a description.
“The real question is not whether …, but how …” moves the discussion on: a strong B2 phrase.
The opinion ends with conditions, not a simple yes or no. That is more balanced and easier to defend.

tasks.title: At the recycling centre
tasks.blurb: Sorting, collecting, throwing away, and whether it really helps.
tasks.imageNeeded: A recycling centre: a big sign saying “Recycling only”, piles of flattened cardboard boxes and blue recycling bins.
tasks.prompt: Describe the picture briefly and then give your opinion.
bullets: What can you see in the picture?
How does recycling work where you live?
Why don't some people sort their rubbish?
Does recycling at home really help, or does the problem need to be solved somewhere else?
How do people deal with rubbish in your country?
phrases: The picture shows …
Where I live, the system works like this: …
A common argument against this is that …
That may be true, but …
What would really make a difference is …
Compared with this, in … people …
tasks.model: The picture shows a recycling centre. There's a big sign that says “Recycling only”, and under it there's a huge pile of cardboard boxes and some blue recycling bins. Where I live, the system works like this: you sort your rubbish at home into different bins, for example paper and card, cans and plastic bottles, food waste, and everything else. The council collects them from outside your house, and anything that doesn't fit in the bins, like old furniture, goes to a recycling centre like this one. A common argument against this is that it isn't worth the effort, because a lot of it gets burnt or sent abroad anyway. That may be true for some plastics, but glass and metal can be recycled again and again, and paper several times. What would really make a difference, though, is producing less packaging in the first place. Recycling limits the damage; it doesn't solve the problem. Compared with this, in my country people hardly sort their rubbish at all, but they also throw away much less, because things get repaired.
check: A system is explained, not just judged.
The counter-argument and your answer to it are both there.
“Recycling limits the damage; it doesn't solve the problem”: a short, sharp sentence at the end stays with the listener.
The comparison with your own country doesn't judge; it describes a difference.
